executive_summary: EUR/JPY sits at 181.14181 as of the price payload's spotDate of 2026-09-03, two sessions after the 2026-09-01 valuation date, and that two-session gap is the single most consequential fact in this report: the pair fell 4.58 yen, or 2.47%, across 2 and 3 September, closing 183.93854 and then 181.14181 after trading as low as 180.52504. Performance is -0.63% over one month, -1.94% over three, -1.53% over six and +4.22% over twelve, so a positive annual number now conceals a market that has made lower highs since the 187.9575 fifty-two-week peak and has spent half a year going nowhere before breaking down. The dominant bilateral narrative is that both central banks are hiking simultaneously — the ECB at 2.25% and the BoJ at 1.00% for a +125bp differential — and the pair therefore turns not on who moves but on whose path is furthest from what is discounted. The euro leg is priced to its plausible ceiling at a 2.75% terminal; the yen leg implies roughly 1.21% after 18 December against an economist consensus centred on 1.75%, and a rush to unwind yen-funded carry trades sent the yen to a one-month high against the dollar after hawkish comments from Governor Ueda and board member Takata raised the possibility of an outsized increase at the 18 September meeting. That is the strategic thesis arriving early and on the tape. The three bilateral differentials that diverge most from the standalone dossiers are the wage composition (euro-area negotiated wages at 2.1% against a third consecutive 5%-plus Japanese shunto), the fiscal inversion (Japan's JPY 36.6trn debt-service line at a 3.8% assumed rate means rising JGB yields are partly a risk premium and therefore not yen-positive), and the pair's own skew at -1.84 volatility points, more negative than USD/JPY's -1.74. The settled verdict is tactically Bullish at conviction 2 (score +0.1049) and strategically Bearish at conviction 3 (score -0.3150); the caveat we state plainly rather than bury is that the tactical Bullish was scored without sight of the 3 September break and now looks the weaker half of the call, while the strategic Bearish looks, if anything, under-scored.

market_context.valuation_assessment: There is no usable PPP series for this cross, and the REER-relative proxy carried in the JPY dossier is worth stating precisely because it is so extreme and so useless for timing: the euro's BIS real broad effective rate of 102.69 against the yen's 65.3 implies a -36.41% real-exchange-rate gap and a mechanical EUR/JPY of 117.93 at REER parity. At 181.14181 the pair trades roughly 53.6% above that figure. That is a base-period artefact measured against 2020, not a fair value, and it should be read as a magnitude constraint on the bull case rather than a signal — the yen has been the cheapest major currency in the world on this measure for three years and it has told you nothing about any four-week window in that period. The genuinely actionable valuation observation is positional rather than absolute: at the 57th closing percentile of its fifty-two-week range and 3.44% below an all-time high, the pair carries no valuation cushion on the topside and a great deal of unpriced room below, because the store finds no clustered price memory whatsoever between 181.30 and 173.39. What is priced at 181.14181 is a persistent +125bp differential and a carry regime that continues to function; what is not priced anywhere in the level is a differential that compresses toward 75-100bp.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime has been one of failed recoveries inside a topping structure. The 30 July to 3 August sessions delivered a 4.5% collapse from 187.415 to a 179.14481 low as Japan's record yen-buying operations landed, and the pair then retraced the whole of it over sixteen sessions to close 185.86987 on 25 August. That recovery has now failed: 185.71927 on 1 September, 183.93854 on 2 September and 181.14181 on 3 September, with the intraday low of 180.52504 holding above the 3 August low of 179.14481 — a higher low inside a clear sequence of lower highs from 187.9575 in April to 187.48 in July to 185.87 in August. The dominant narrative underneath has changed from a functioning positive-carry cross to the expression of a repricing BoJ, with State Street's Masahiko Loo framing the structural shift as Japan gradually ceasing to be the marginal buyer of foreign bonds.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The bilateral policy differential is +125bp, with the ECB deposit facility at 2.25% and the BoJ overnight call target at around 1.00%, both as of 2026-09-01. In pip terms that is 226 pips of annualised carry at spot 181.14181, or 18.9 pips per month, against an ATR(14) of 95 pips — so a single average day's range consumes roughly five months of accrued carry, and the 365-pip 3 September session wiped out nineteen months of it. That ratio, more than any level, is why this pair is a directional trade wearing a carry costume. Carry-to-volatility is roughly +0.18-0.19 on the payload's own (documented low-biased) 3-month implied estimate; because the volatility input runs low by a median 14.4%, the true ratio is worse on every adjusted measure. On every measure this is the least efficient positive-carry expression available to the euro — the euro dossier's own independent computation of +0.19 is the most generous reading obtainable and still ranks below EUR/CHF at +0.58. The carry regime has been working (VIX 14.51, IG spreads 79bp, HY 263bp, record equities) and has just begun to stop — it broke once already this year during the 31 July joint intervention and reassembled within a month, but this time the trigger is a rate path rather than an official flow, which is the distinction that determines durability. Forward points at spot 181.14181 are -22.6 pips at 1m (outright 180.916), -68.5 pips at 3m (outright 180.456) and -137.1 pips at 6m (outright 179.771); the forward curve discounts the pair by 151.8bp per year, 26.8bp wider than the 125bp policy differential, with the wedge being the cross-currency basis (corroborated by the JPY dossier's independent derivation of roughly -23bp). A long position expressed in forwards accrues 152bp rather than 125bp and the basis works in its favour, while a short position pays the extra 27bp.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral policy differential is +125bp in the euro's favour (ECB deposit facility 2.25%, BoJ overnight call target around 1.00%), and the gated rate block confirms both legs as of 2026-09-01. The defining tactical fact is symmetry: the ECB is roughly 97% priced to move to 2.50% on 10 September and the BoJ is roughly 80-90% priced to move to 1.25% on 18 September, so if both deliver as discounted the differential ends the tactical window exactly where it started. A differential that is unchanged after two fully-priced decisions eight days apart cannot carry a directional stance. The 10-year leg is thinner than the policy leg and points the other way: the payload gives a +30bp Bund-JGB differential on the consistent 2026-06-01 monthly series, and on live levels the JGB touching 3.00% on 1 September against a Bund at 3.29-3.30% compresses that toward roughly 29bp, a cross-dated approximation flagged as such. Transmission into the pair is via the carry channel, and at +125bp against a 3-month at-the-money implied volatility of 6.838% the carry-to-vol ratio is only +0.18 — the euro's own dossier calls this the least efficient of its positive-carry expressions. Level favours long EUR/JPY, trajectory and pricing skew favour short; over four weeks they cancel.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two legs stop being symmetric and the differential compresses. The euro leg is fully priced and arguably over-priced: the strip carries a 2.75% terminal by February 2027, which the euro dossier itself judges 15-25bp too high against a negotiated wage tracker at 2.1% for Q2 2026 and the ECB's own projection of 2.0% inflation in 2028. The yen leg is the opposite — the OIS curve implies only about 1.21% after the 18 December BoJ meeting, one hike and essentially nothing more inside 2026, while half of 36 surveyed economists now put terminal at 1.75% and 35 of 54 expect at least 1.50% by end-March 2027. If the ECB stalls at 2.50-2.625% and the BoJ reaches 1.50-1.75%, the differential narrows from 125bp toward 75-100bp, a 25-50bp compression that removes a fifth to two-fifths of the carry supporting a long position. The scheduled decisions that would do it are named: the BoJ Outlook Report on 30 October and the 18 December meeting on the yen side, the 17 December ECB projections round on the euro side. The 10-year leg reinforces the direction — at roughly 30bp the Bund-JGB gap is already the flattest relationship in the euro's benchmarking set and the euro dossier identifies its narrowness as the principal risk to the cross.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation differential is roughly 100bp in the euro area's favour and the data-surprise differential runs the same way. Euro-area HICP printed 2.9% headline and 2.5% core in July with services at 3.3%, and the August flash consensus was 3.3% headline after Spanish HICP at 4.5%, French at 2.7% and Belgian CPI at 3.97% all surprised upward. Japan printed 1.9% headline and 1.8% core for July on the new 2025 base, with Tokyo August at 1.9% and 1.8%. On activity the euro area is also the positive-surprise economy: German Ifo at 88.8 against 87.2 expected, flash composite PMI 52.1 with new orders at a 40-month high, German Q2 GDP beating at +0.3% quarter-on-quarter. Japan's Q2 GDP rose only 0.3% quarter-on-quarter, 1.1% annualised against a 2.0% consensus, with private consumption contributing nothing for the first time in eight quarters and business investment down 1.2%. Growth differential: euro area 1.0% year-on-year against Japan 0.55%. Transmission is through the relative reaction function — the euro-area data flow currently gives the ECB more reason to keep tightening than the Japanese data flow gives the BoJ, which supports the pair over four weeks. The asymmetry to watch is that Japan's 17 September national CPI lands inside the window and carries a mechanical upside skew from the energy-subsidy unwind.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the composition of each inflation matters more than its level, and the composition reverses the ranking. Euro-area inflation is imported cost-push: energy contributed +0.94pp of the 2.9% July headline at +10.0% year-on-year, while food and processed food decelerated sharply and negotiated wages printed 2.1% for Q2 2026 against 3.2% in 2025, converging on the 2013-2024 average. Wages at 2.1% cannot sustain services at 3.3%. Japanese inflation is wage-supported: the 2026 shunto delivered 5.01% for a third consecutive year above 5%, real wages have been positive for six straight months, nominal earnings above 3% for five months, and the BoJ's own ex-special-factors measure sits at 2.3% with the trimmed mean at 2.0% — the 50bp wedge to the official 1.8% core being government energy and education subsidies that the Board expects to unwind, taking core clearly above 2% from the second half of fiscal 2026. So the euro's inflation is set to fade with energy base effects while Japan's is set to accelerate as suppression rolls off, and the relative reaction functions move accordingly. Growth is the offsetting consideration and it favours the euro area, at 1.0% against 0.55% with Japanese consumption flat — which is why confidence is 54 rather than higher.

factors.horizon_split: Bullish tactically and Bearish strategically, and the mechanism is level-versus-composition. Over four weeks the pair is paid for the LEVEL of the inflation gap and the direction of surprises, both of which currently favour the euro area by roughly 100bp and a clean run of beats. Over one to six months the pair is paid for PERSISTENCE, and persistence requires wages: at 2.1% the euro area does not have them and at 5.01% Japan does. The inflection is arithmetic on both sides — euro-area energy base effects roll out while Japanese subsidy suppression rolls off.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: EUR/JPY sits in the framework's moderate risk-sensitivity band, and the asymmetry is structural: the yen has the strongest negative correlation to VIX in the G10 and is the funding currency of first resort, while the euro is a non-haven mid-carry currency that performs best in exactly the calm, dollar-soft regime now prevailing. The cross-asset state is close to the best possible configuration for the pair. VIX closed at 14.51 on 27 August, down 3.70 points on the month after touching a 2026 low of 14.13. US investment-grade spreads are 79bp and high yield 263bp, the latter 21bp tighter on the month, with the Federal Reserve Chair himself describing spreads as near the low end of their historical ranges. Euro Stoxx 50 set a record above 6,560 and the Nikkei is up 58.4% over twelve months. The Fed's broad trade-weighted dollar index fell 2.1% over the month, which opens the anti-dollar channel the euro benefits from most. Transmission is direct and one-directional: in this regime capital borrows yen and buys higher-yielding assets, and the euro at 2.25% is on the receiving side of that flow relative to a 1.00% yen. Confidence is capped at 58 because the calm is measurably one-sided and the Hormuz situation escalated on 30-31 August.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the risk factor becomes a distribution question rather than a state question, and for this pair the distribution is genuinely two-sided. The modal path is persistence, which is bullish: if VIX stays near 14 and credit near 79bp, the yen keeps funding and the pair keeps grinding. But the tail is asymmetric in the other direction and it is larger for EUR/JPY than for most crosses, because the two legs sit at opposite ends of the haven spectrum — in a genuine risk-off the yen is bought and the euro, which is not a haven, is sold, so the pair takes both legs of the move rather than one. The identified regime-break catalysts are dated: a 30 September US appropriations deadline in a year that has already seen two federal shutdowns, US midterms on 3 November, and a Hormuz situation that escalated as recently as 31 August. The historical analogue is the August 2024 carry unwind, in which yen crosses moved violently from a positioning base the JPY dossier describes as more extreme than today's. Modal-bullish against tail-bearish, with the tail unusually fat for this specific pair, is a Neutral rather than a compromise.

Tactically the factor measures the prevailing regime, and the prevailing regime — low volatility, tight credit, record equities, a softening broad dollar — is the one in which a yen-funded mid-carry cross performs best. strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the futures data stops being the relevant dataset and the structural flow becomes bilaterally specific in a way that is genuinely rare for a cross. Japanese institutions are large holders of euro-area sovereign debt — the Banque de France records Japan holding around 6% of total outstanding OATs at end-2022 — and the JPY dossier identifies EUR/JPY as one of only two currencies in which Japanese foreign bond portfolios are concentrated. Japanese life-insurer hedge ratios are at historically low levels on both Daiwa's FY2026 survey and a Bank of Japan Review, which means an unusually high share of any repatriation or hedge-ratio normalisation lands in spot rather than rolling off existing forwards, and it is EUR/JPY spot that absorbs part of it. The trigger is a normal consequence of the base case rather than a shock: rising Japanese yields and improving hedged returns are exactly the conditions under which the calculus flips, and the observable evidence has already begun — Japanese residents sold a net JPY 1,978.4bn of foreign bonds and JPY 869.0bn of foreign equities in the reference week 16-22 August, a JPY 5.5trn week-on-week swing, and Japanese investors sold USD 29.6bn of US debt in Q1 2026 while the Finance Minister publicly sought greater domestic allocation by pension funds. The euro-side offset is real but smaller: a residual -36,352 speculative short in a currency whose central bank is tightening, and a euro reserve share that fell to 20.03% in Q1 2026, which cuts the other way.

factors.horizon_split: Neutral tactically and Bearish strategically because the two relevant datasets run on different clocks. Over four weeks the dataset is CFTC futures, and with both legs short at the 30th-33rd percentile after both squeezes have already been taken there is genuinely no signal. Over one to six months the dataset is Japanese institutional allocation, and there the flow is one-directional and bilaterally specific: Japanese holders of euro-area bonds normalising hedge ratios from historic lows are a direct EUR/JPY seller with no euro-side equivalent. Confidence is only 53 because the timing of hedge-ratio normalisation is genuinely unknowable and credible research argues repatriation is slow and already partly priced.

tactical.combined_positioning_signal: Short EUR and short JPY at the 30th and 33rd percentiles respectively — the two legs offset and the implied EUR/JPY spec position is close to flat, so the contrarian trigger is absent by construction rather than by judgement.
tactical.unwind_trigger: A BoJ hike on 18 September delivered with explicit acceleration language, taking December pricing from roughly 1.21% implied toward 1.46% while the ECB has already spent its 10 September event — that repositions the differential from the leg the market is least prepared for.
tactical.historical_analogue: The July 2026 intervention episode: a record joint operation forced 41,165 contracts of yen covering in one week and moved yen crosses hard, and within four weeks more than half the move had been given back — yen-positive positional shocks in this cycle have had a half-life under a month.
tactical.contrarian_case: The case against our own Neutral is that the market has now watched the yen fail to hold gains through a record joint intervention, a delivered BoJ hike and a 30-year high in JGB yields, and has rationally concluded that yen rallies are for selling. On that reading the correct response to any EUR/JPY dip is to add length, and the positioning data — moderately short both legs with open interest in the yen contract 26% below its June peak — is consistent with a market that has already tested and rejected the bearish case.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: Mildly bearish for the pair, and not because of the visible short but because of the invisible one: Japanese institutional length in euro-area bonds held at historically low hedge ratios is a latent EUR/JPY seller that appears in no positioning dataset.
strategic.unwind_trigger: The BoJ reaching 1.50-1.75% while hedging costs improve, making JGBs competitive with hedged euro-area paper — Reuters reporting from an earlier episode of the same mechanism noted that a further rise in Japanese yields would prompt domestic investors to unwind overseas investments, particularly in European bonds.
strategic.historical_analogue: The August 2024 carry unwind, in which yen crosses moved violently from a CFTC base the JPY dossier describes as more extreme than today's — a warning as much as a template, since today's 33rd-percentile short has room to build further before any unwind begins.
strategic.contrarian_case: The strongest counter is credible and well-sourced: Capital Economics asks directly whether rising JGB yields will cause capital repatriation and argues that with unhedged yield gaps still favouring overseas bonds and hedged returns improving as other central banks ease, Japanese investors will not respond to higher JGB yields by repatriating; other analysis notes overseas positions built over decades will not turn on a dime, with the story being not large-scale repatriation but Japan gradually ceasing to be the marginal buyer. If that is right, the structural seller never arrives, the -36,352 euro short converts to length as the ECB delivers, and the pair's positive carry does the rest — which is why this factor carries only 53 confidence and a 0.06 weight.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the rare pair in which both legs are large net energy importers buying into the same supply shock, so the question is not whether the shock hurts but which leg it hurts more. On the framework's own commodity direction rules the answer is the yen: oil up is a double-negative for JPY against a single-negative for EUR, LNG up is a double-negative for JPY with no EUR entry, and TTF up is a single-negative for EUR. The data corroborates the ranking. Japan's terms-of-trade index collapsed from 90.5 in Q1 2026 to 83.8 in Q2 and 81.62 in July, a 9.8% fall in two quarters, with mineral fuels at 22.1% of all imports and up 53.5% year-on-year on falling volumes, and June produced Japan's first monthly current-account deficit in seventeen months. The euro area's deterioration is real but smaller and slower: the twelve-month current-account surplus fell from 2.0% to 1.7% of GDP with the goods surplus down EUR 60bn, and it remains a surplus of EUR 282bn on goods while Japan's goods account has turned to deficit. The bilateral trade relationship itself is close to irrelevant as a driver — EUR exports to JPY of USD 63.7bn against imports of USD 60.1bn for a net EUR balance of just USD 3.6bn in 2024 — so the transmission is entirely through the third-party energy bill rather than through direct flows. Two dated releases fall inside the window on the Japanese side: the July balance of payments on 8 September and August trade statistics mid-month.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months this is the heaviest factor in the table at 0.16, and it is honestly balanced — which is why it earns a zero rather than a small number. The bearish-yen case is that Japan's terms of trade have already fallen 9.8% in two quarters, that it imports essentially all of its hydrocarbons with JKM LNG up 101.9% year-on-year, and that its H1 record current-account surplus of JPY 17.43trn is 27.6 times more primary income than goods surplus, so it generates far less spot demand than the headline implies. The bearish-euro case is equally specific and it is the euro dossier's highest-conviction negative: EU gas storage at 62.99% on 24 August against an effectively closed Strait of Hormuz, TTF above EUR 70/MWh for the first time since January 2023, and Goldman Sachs warning that current prices will not be enough to manage storage through winter with December TTF possibly needing to exceed EUR 100/MWh. Each dossier assigns this factor its strongest strategic negative at almost identical confidence, 66 for EUR and 64 for JPY. Bilaterally that is a wash: Japan's damage is realised and larger in magnitude, the euro area's is prospective and larger in tail, and the euro area retains a headline surplus while Japan retains a record one. Netting two roughly equal negatives to a directional stance would be manufacturing a view from thin evidence.

factors.horizon_split: Bullish tactically and Neutral strategically. Tactically the pair responds to the monthly flow news, and Japan's is deteriorating faster on every observable measure while two Japanese releases land inside the window. Strategically the weight nearly triples to 0.16 and the comparison becomes cumulative rather than marginal, at which point the euro area's dated winter gas test — 62.99% storage, a closed Hormuz, a possible EUR 100/MWh December — matches Japan's realised terms-of-trade collapse in force. Two near-equal negatives net to zero, and a zero at 0.16 weight is a real analytical statement rather than an absence of one.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: EUR: the world's largest net energy importer as a bloc, with Dutch TTF natural gas the critical exposure. TTF up is negative EUR and oil up is negative EUR. Energy contributed +0.94pp of the 2.9% July HICP at +10.0% year-on-year, and the goods surplus fell EUR 60bn over twelve months. No commodity export offset of any size.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: JPY: imports essentially all of its hydrocarbons. Oil up is a DOUBLE negative for JPY, LNG (JKM) up is a DOUBLE negative for JPY, and there is no positive commodity entry anywhere. Mineral fuels were 22.1% of July imports and rose 53.5% year-on-year on falling volumes; JKM is up 101.9% year-on-year and Newcastle coal sits at USD 141.75 a tonne.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Step 1, oil — the rules give −− for JPY against − for EUR, so a rise damages the quote leg more than the base leg and the pair RISES. Step 2, LNG (JKM) — the rules give −− for JPY and carry no EUR entry, so a rise again damages the quote leg more and the pair RISES; JKM is the fastest-moving of the three at +101.9% year-on-year. Step 3, TTF natural gas — the rules give − for EUR and no JPY entry, so a rise damages the base leg and the pair FALLS; TTF above EUR 70/MWh is the euro area's acute exposure. Net across the three legs: two of the three energy vectors point the pair higher and the third points it lower, so the direction rules produce a modest bullish net for EUR/JPY. The realised data agrees on magnitude — Japan's terms of trade fell 9.8% in two quarters against a euro-area current-account deterioration of 0.3pp of GDP — which is why the tactical stance is Bullish. What flattens this to Neutral strategically is that the TTF leg is the one with a dated, quantified escalation path (62.99% storage into winter, a possible EUR 100/MWh December), while the oil and LNG legs have no comparable dated catalyst, so the base-leg damage is more likely to accelerate from here than the quote-leg damage.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Pair rises modestly. Oil up is −− for JPY and − for EUR on the direction rules, so Japan's import bill and terms of trade deteriorate faster than the euro area's; the offset is that higher oil typically drags TTF and JKM with it, and the JKM leg is also −− for JPY while the TTF leg is − for EUR, so the composite still favours the pair. Net: bullish EUR/JPY, but less cleanly than the oil leg alone suggests.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Pair falls modestly. Both legs benefit, but the quote leg benefits more because it carries the double-negative exposure that is being removed; Japan's terms of trade would recover from 81.62 toward the mid-80s while the euro area's improvement runs mainly through the gas curve, which is the slower and stickier of the two. Net: bearish EUR/JPY, and this is the branch in which the euro's own dossier expects its rate cycle to be killed as well.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: JKM LNG, with Dutch TTF a close second. JKM at +101.9% year-on-year is the single fastest-moving input and it is the only one of the three that hits the quote leg with no base-leg entry at all, so it is the cleanest source of directional bilateral signal; TTF is the input most likely to change the ranking, because it is the one with a dated winter escalation path against 62.99% EU storage.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Receives 0.02 at both horizons, funded by the Factor 10 non-USD-cross reduction. Both central banks are hiking simultaneously with decisions eight days apart in September and one day apart in October and December, so the pair's direction turns on which bank's communicated pace is furthest from what is discounted, and the gated calendar repeatedly gives the quote leg the last word.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks are communicating hawkishly and both have clean recent delivery records, so credibility is not the differentiator — the gap between guidance and pricing is. The ECB has closed its gap completely: the July Account, published 27 August, twice described the hold as a pause and said it was important not to signal the end of tightening, and the market responded by pricing 10 September at roughly 97%. There is nothing left to arbitrage at that meeting, and the euro dossier flags a tonal risk in the other direction if Lagarde repeats her July acknowledgement that there is no clear evidence of second-round effects. The BoJ's gap is wide open. The 10 August Summary of Opinions states that the pace of hikes will be faster than market expectations and that it is necessary to accelerate the pace of adjustment; Takata dissented in July in favour of moving to 1.25%; Ueda has said the impact of currency volatility on inflation may be growing; Deputy Governor Himino called on 27 August for timely rate rises and linked a weak yen to faster inflation. Against that the market prices only about 1.21% after 18 December. Sequencing compounds it: the ECB reports first on 10 September and the BoJ speaks last on 18 September, so the final tactical word belongs to the leg with the unpriced pace language.

tactical.what_is_priced: The ECB's hawkishness is priced to its plausible ceiling and the BoJ's is priced well below its own stated intent, so the September pair of meetings has more capacity to surprise on the yen leg than on the euro leg.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the guidance divergence becomes the second-largest force in the table and it points one way. The BoJ has changed its stated objective rather than merely its tone: the July Outlook replaced the goal of lifting inflation toward 2% with stabilising it and preventing an upward deviation, which converts every upside inflation surprise from a milestone into a tightening impulse, and it revised FY2027 core CPI UP to 2.4% while attributing the FY2026 cut to temporary subsidies. It also abolished the interim assessment of its bond-purchase plan, so balance-sheet changes now occur ad hoc at meetings, raising the probability of an unscheduled hawkish surprise. The ECB has moved the other way in substance if not in tone: its own negotiated wage tracker at 2.1% and its own 2028 projection of 2.0% inflation sit awkwardly against a market-priced 2.75% terminal, and the euro dossier's own strategic Guidance stance is Neutral precisely because the market has extrapolated further than the institution's arithmetic supports. The gated calendar makes the asymmetry concrete: the BoJ has a projection round on 30 October while the ECB's 29 October meeting carries none, and on 17-18 December the ECB projections land one day before the BoJ decision. The euro area's likely December revision is downward as energy base effects enter the 2027-28 window; Japan's October and January revisions skew upward.

strategic.what_is_priced: The strip prices the ECB's guidance being sustained to a demanding terminal and the BoJ's being delivered at half its stated pace; both errors run in the same direction for this pair.

factors.horizon_split: Bearish at both horizons with confidence rising from 57 to 60 as the weight rises from 0.09 to 0.14, because guidance operates on expectations and expectations take months to reprice. Tactically only the accompanying language of two already-priced decisions is in play, and the BoJ happens to speak last. Strategically the reframed BoJ objective, the upward-revised FY2027 forecast, the abolition of scheduled balance-sheet assessments and a calendar that gives the quote leg the projection round in late October compound into a systematically wider gap between guidance and pricing on the yen side than on the euro side.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The single most asymmetric event risk in this pair is intervention, and it only ever runs one way. Japan bought roughly JPY 27.1trn of yen during 2026, including JPY 15,399.3bn between 30 July and 26 August and a joint operation with the US Treasury on 31 July, against a previous full-year record of JPY 15.32trn in 2024 and zero in 2025. The Finance Minister has said Japan will not hesitate to intervene jointly again and that it plans to use the Federal Reserve's FIMA repo facility; the US Treasury Secretary repeated the commitment at the G20 on 31 August. Yen-buying intervention is executed against the dollar but drags every yen cross, so EUR/JPY is a collateral casualty with no equivalent official bid or offer on the euro side — there is a well-capitalised, publicly committed buyer of the quote currency and nobody at all defending the base. On the euro side the tactical event set is unhelpful rather than helpful: France heads into a 2027 budget battle with a fragmented parliament and Fitch affirmed A+ on 28 August with an explicit deficit warning. The shared Hormuz escalation of 30-31 August cuts against the yen through the import bill but that channel is Factor 5; here the official-flow asymmetry dominates and it is bearish for the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the event channel becomes genuinely two-sided and the honest answer is a zero. The intervention option remains on the yen side and has now been demonstrated as bilateral policy with US participation, which raises both its probability and its potential scale — but its demonstrated half-life in this cycle is under a month, as the July episode showed. The Hormuz situation is the largest shared risk and it is symmetric in sign but not in magnitude: escalation damages both legs through energy, with the quote leg more exposed on volumes and the base leg more exposed on the dated winter gas balance; de-escalation restores the euro area's terms of trade while also killing the ECB's hiking cycle, which is the specific reason the euro dossier calls that branch net euro-positive and this pair calls it ambiguous. Against that, the euro leg carries a one-sided domestic political risk that Japan does not: France is the euro area's fragility trade now rather than Italy, the 2027 budget must pass a parliament that has not passed structural reform, and the EU's retaliatory-tariff pause expires in early February 2027. Japan by contrast has no scheduled national election inside the horizon after the February 2026 supermajority. One-sided euro political risk against a one-sided yen official bid is a balance.

factors.horizon_split: Bearish tactically and Neutral strategically because the intervention asymmetry is a near-dated phenomenon while the political and energy risks are persistent and two-sided. Over four weeks a publicly committed, bilaterally capable yen bid with no euro-side counterpart dominates and it points one way. Over six months that option remains but its demonstrated half-life is under a month, and the euro area's one-sided French fiscal and political risk grows into the 2027 budget process, so the two roughly cancel.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The fiscal differential is unusually wide and it is currently repricing on the quote side only. Japan's FY2027 ministry budget requests, submitted 31 August, total roughly JPY 143trn with a record JPY 36.6trn debt-service line struck on an assumed interest rate raised to 3.8% from 3.0% — debt service alone is about a quarter of the request. The market is responding: the 10-year JGB touched 3.00% on 1 September for the first time since 1996, the 2-year hit a 31-year high, the 25s30s spread is inverted at -1.0bp, and the 28 August 2-year auction drew a bid-to-cover of 2.97 against a twelve-month average of 3.74. The euro area's fiscal picture is the opposite kind of quiet: OAT-Bund at 83.6bp and BTP-Bund at roughly 81-85bp are contained, Italy has been re-rated to Baa2 after seven upgrades, auctions are clearing normally, and the Bund at a fifteen-year high reflects genuine term-premium repricing alongside stable peripheral spreads. The transmission into the pair is the JPY dossier's central insight inverted: a rise in JGB yields driven by fiscal risk premium rather than policy expectation carries no currency-positive content, which is exactly why the yen failed to rally through a 30-year yield high. A weak 3 September 30-year auction would therefore be bullish for this pair, not bearish.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the fiscal differential is the clearest structural argument for the pair, and it is one of the few places where a third-party observer states the bilateral comparison directly: DWS noted in July 2026 that euro-area bonds remained more attractive than JGBs on the higher policy rate, and that debt sustainability was more of a concern for Japan given a debt-to-GDP ratio above 200% against roughly 81% for Germany. The arithmetic behind that is the interaction with Factor 1. Japan's debt-service line rose JPY 5.36trn in a single budget cycle when the assumed rate went from 3.0% to 3.8%, so each further 100bp of BoJ tightening costs roughly JPY 5trn — which means the yen's rate cycle is self-limiting in a way the euro's is not, and it is the mechanism that converts a hiking central bank into a fiscal risk premium. Supply is rising as the dominant buyer withdraws: BoJ JGB purchases step down from JPY 2.5trn a month to JPY 2.1trn by Q1 2027. The euro area's structure is materially better: German fiscal expansion is large but is being absorbed with peripheral spreads stable, Italy has moved from liability to asset, and the fat left tail is France rather than the bloc. The offset, and the reason confidence is 60 rather than higher, is that roughly 90% of JGBs are domestically held with the BoJ owning about half, which caps rollover risk, and all three major agencies still rate Japan stable.

Tactically the factor is expressed through two Japanese auctions and a budget headline, all known and partly discounted. Strategically it becomes compounding arithmetic — roughly JPY 5trn of additional debt service per 100bp of BoJ tightening, against a purchase programme stepping down from JPY 2.5trn to JPY 2.1trn a month — which is the mechanism that caps how far the quote leg's rate cycle can run and is the single most important offset to the Bearish Factor 1 and Factor 6 readings.

The at-the-money surface says the opposite kind of nothing: the gated payload gives 6.469% at 38.6 days, 6.838% at 94.7 days and 7.104% at 185.7 days — clean contango with no hump despite the ECB on 10 September and the BoJ on 18 September both falling inside the front tenor, and despite the payload's own warning that the triangle method understates by a median 14.4%. A flat surface with an extreme skew says: low probability of a large move, but if there is one it is pair-down.

strategic.rationale: At strategic weights this becomes a coherent one-direction call rather than a contest. Policy and Guidance carry 0.40 of the weight between them and both point the same way for the same reason: the euro leg's rate story is fully monetised and the yen leg's is not. The euro strip carries a 2.75% ECB terminal by February 2027, which the euro's own dossier judges 15-25bp too high against a negotiated wage tracker at 2.1% and a 2028 projection of 2.0% inflation, while the yen curve implies only about 1.21% after 18 December against an economist distribution in which half of 36 respondents name 1.75% and 35 of 54 expect at least 1.50% by end-March 2027. If the ECB stalls at 2.50-2.625% and the BoJ reaches 1.50-1.75%, the 125bp differential compresses toward 75-100bp and a quarter to two fifths of the carry supporting the cross disappears. The guidance evidence reinforces the rates evidence rather than duplicating it: the BoJ has reframed its objective to preventing an upward deviation from 2%, revised FY2027 core CPI up to 2.4%, abolished scheduled balance-sheet assessments, and had a Board member dissent in favour of moving faster, while the ECB's own account leaves it dependent on wages that are not there. Inflation composition says the same thing from a third angle — the euro's overshoot is energy base effects that reverse, Japan's is a third consecutive 5%-plus shunto with subsidy suppression that unwinds. Where the two dossiers conflict is instructive: each scores its own external balance as its strongest strategic negative at 66 and 64 confidence, and bilaterally that cancels to zero at a 0.16 weight, which is why the heaviest cell in this table is empty rather than decisive. The bilateral modifiers are the repatriation channel, specific to this pair rather than generic — Japan has held around 6% of outstanding French OATs, Japanese life-insurer hedge ratios sit at historic lows so normalisation lands in spot, and Japanese residents already sold a net JPY 1,978.4bn of foreign bonds in a single August week — and the yen basis, which the same hedge-ratio normalisation would widen. What is priced against what we expect: the market prices the euro path correctly and the yen path conservatively, and pays almost nothing in the volatility surface for the possibility that the compression is a regime rather than an episode. The path of least resistance is a contested, saw-toothed decline in the pair rather than a trend, because the positive carry keeps paying while the differential narrows. consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: Consensus appears to carry forward the assumption that has been correct for two years — that the euro-area rate advantage is durable and the BoJ moves slower than it says. Two things have changed and the proxy does not reflect them. First, the asymmetry of pricing has inverted: the euro's terminal is now priced at or beyond what the ECB's own wage tracker at 2.1% and its own 2.0% projection for 2028 support, while the yen curve implies only about 1.21% after December against an economist consensus centred on 1.75% and a Summary of Opinions that says the pace will exceed market expectations. Where we agree with consensus is the near term, and where we think consensus is right and we may be wrong is on timing — respected research argues Japanese repatriation is slow, hedged and largely priced. Berenberg notes that European sovereign debt has been highly popular among Japanese institutional buyers, with the GPIF alone holding slightly over 1% of the entire German Bund market, and CNBC reports Japanese investors repatriating capital, selling USD 29.6bn of US debt in Q1 2026 alone.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: Capturing a stance-category divergence — a decline the consensus proxy places past twelve months arriving inside six, expressed while the pair's own six-month implied volatility sits barely 0.27 points above its three-month and the yen skew has already decayed from roughly -1.84 at one month to -0.91 at six; in pip terms 647 pips of divergence, or 3.5%, from the six-month consensus
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: Two failure modes: timing risk, where the BoJ pauses after September, the terminal reprices back below 1.50%, and the 125bp carry keeps paying while nothing else happens — at a cost of 486 pips of spot plus 137 pips of carry from a 183.50 average entry; and the empty-cell risk, where a genuine euro-area winter gas squeeze (TTF above EUR 100/MWh, storage below 75%) turns the 0.16-weight external balance factor decisively against the base leg, removing roughly a tenth of the score in one move. The tactical call fails if the BoJ delivers on 18 September with explicit acceleration language while the ECB projections disappoint.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons genuinely diverge, by a full stance category and 0.42 of score, and the divergence is mechanical rather than contradictory — four factors flip sign and two weights move materially. Factor 1 flips from Neutral to Bearish because two fully-priced 25bp hikes eight days apart leave the differential untouched over four weeks but the paths separate over six months. Factor 2 flips from Bullish to Bearish on level-versus-composition. Factor 4 flips from Neutral to Bearish because the relevant dataset changes from CFTC futures to Japanese institutional allocation. Factor 5 flips from Bullish to Neutral as its weight nearly triples and the euro area's dated winter gas test grows to match Japan's realised terms-of-trade collapse. On weights, Factor 2 falls from 0.18 to 0.10 while Factors 5 and 6 rise from 0.06 and 0.09 to 0.16 and 0.14.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: Late October, dated in the gated calendar rather than inferred. The tactical view expires with the September cluster; the first scheduled event that can reprice the strategic view is the pair of decisions on 29-30 October, where the BoJ publishes an Outlook Report while the ECB's meeting the previous day carries none. The 17-18 December pair, with ECB projections one day before the BoJ decision, is the confirmation point.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Treat these as two different positions rather than one position with a long horizon. The tactical Bullish clears its threshold by 0.0049 with 43% of the applied weight contributing zero, so it is a direction to respect and not a view to size — and it is the horizon at which the pair's positive 125bp carry is actually being paid without the differential having narrowed. The strategic Bearish is the higher-conviction call and it is fighting that carry, so timing matters more than direction: the window between the September cluster and the 30 October BoJ Outlook Report is the period in which the pair earns carry with no scheduled catalyst against it, and late October is where the two views hand over. Operationally: hold tactical length small with a stop at 179.00 and a target of 183.20, use any rally into 183.50-185.80 to build the strategic short with a stop above 186.75.

catalysts.event: Japan July balance of payments and revised Q2 GDP
catalysts.rationale: June produced Japan's first monthly current-account deficit in seventeen months and July's trade balance widened 4.1-fold year-on-year on a mineral fuel bill up 53.5%. A second consecutive current-account deficit would be the first back-to-back pair since 2022 and would undercut the structural-surplus assumption that supports the yen leg, which is bullish for the pair. The GDP revision skews upward on a corporate capex beat, which cuts mildly the other way.

catalysts.event: ECB Governing Council decision with new Eurosystem staff projections
catalysts.rationale: A 25bp move to a 2.50% deposit rate is roughly 97% priced, so the decision is not the catalyst — the projection revisions are. With euro-area energy at +10.0% year-on-year an upward revision to the 2026 and 2027 inflation paths from the June baseline is likely and would be read hawkishly for the base leg. The tactical risk runs the other way if Lagarde repeats her July acknowledgement that there is no clear evidence of second-round effects, which would be a sell-the-fact for the pair.

catalysts.event: Japan August corporate goods price index and terms-of-trade update
catalysts.rationale: This release produces the terms-of-trade index that fell from 90.5 in Q1 to 81.62 in July, and July's yen-basis import prices rose 29.1% year-on-year against 17.7% in contract-currency terms. With JKM LNG up 101.9% year-on-year and Brent above USD 90, August should deteriorate further, which is a direct income transfer out of the quote economy with no equivalent on the base leg at monthly frequency.

July printed 1.8% core against a BoJ ex-special-factors measure of 2.3%, a 50bp wedge that is entirely government energy and education subsidies the Board expects to unwind. Tokyo core has accelerated three consecutive months and the 2025 rebasing lowered the year-ago base. A core print at or above 2.0% would be the first at target since January and would take the 18 September hike from likely to certain while lifting terminal pricing, compressing the differential and pressuring the pair.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting decision
catalysts.rationale: The largest single event in the tactical window and the last word of the September cluster, eight days after the ECB. A 25bp move to 1.25% is roughly 80-90% priced, so the transmission runs through the press conference rather than the decision: December pricing implies only about 1.21%, and if Ueda repeats the Summary of Opinions formulation that the pace will exceed market expectations, a second hike moves from lightly priced to discounted and the 125bp differential starts compressing. Ueda and Takata have already raised the possibility of an outsized increase at this meeting, so the distribution now includes a 50bp move.

catalysts.event: US FY2027 appropriations deadline coinciding with the Japanese interim fiscal half-year end
catalysts.rationale: Two coincident events that both work against the pair. A US shutdown is precedented, with two already in 2026, and would be risk-negative — in which the yen is bought as a haven and the euro sold as a non-haven, so the pair takes both legs of the move. Separately the Japanese interim book close generates documented repatriation and dividend-related flows, and with life-insurer hedge ratios at historic lows an unusually high share lands in spot.

catalysts.event: ECB Governing Council decision (no staff projections)
catalysts.rationale: A non-projection meeting six weeks after the September move, and the base case is a hold at 2.50%. Because the market prices a 2.75% terminal by February 2027, the language carries the information: a hold framed as another pause sustains the terminal and supports the pair, while a hold framed as data-dependent with softening wage commentary begins the downward repricing that drives the strategic bearish case. This meeting has no projection round while the BoJ's the following day does.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting decision with quarterly Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: The single most asymmetric scheduled event in this pair's calendar: the quote leg gets a full projection round one day after a base-leg meeting that has none. The July Outlook already revised FY2027 core CPI up to 2.4% and described price risks as skewed to the upside, and the October vintage will incorporate a further terms-of-trade shock and a subsidy unwind. Outlook revisions are consistently under-anticipated and this one skews upward, which pressures the pair through both the rate and guidance channels.

catalysts.event: Northern-hemisphere heating season test of the 62.99% EU gas storage level recorded on 24 August
catalysts.rationale: Dated to the week rather than the day because it is a physical rather than a scheduled event. Both legs are large net energy importers taking the same Hormuz shock, and this is the one channel where the base leg is more exposed than the quote leg: TTF above EUR 70/MWh against storage well below seasonal norms, with Goldman Sachs warning December TTF may need to exceed EUR 100/MWh. This is the specific development capable of turning the strategic table's empty 0.16-weight external balance cell against the base leg.

catalysts.event: ECB Governing Council decision with new Eurosystem staff projections
catalysts.rationale: The pivotal base-leg event of the strategic horizon, and it lands one day before the BoJ. This is the first projection round in which 2026 energy base effects come clearly into the 2027 and 2028 forecast window; a downward revision to the 2027 path removes the justification for the market's 2.75% terminal and reprices the euro strip lower, which is precisely the compression the strategic Bearish stance rests on. If instead second-round effects finally appear in the wage and services paths, the terminal holds and the stance should be revisited.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting decision
catalysts.rationale: On current pricing the market implies only about 1.21% after this meeting, meaning a second 2026 hike is barely discounted, while half of 36 surveyed economists put terminal at 1.75% and 35 of 54 expect at least 1.50% by end-March 2027. A December move would therefore be a genuine repricing rather than a confirmation, and it lands one day after the ECB projections — the same sequencing asymmetry that runs through this pair's whole calendar, with the quote leg speaking last.

catalysts.event: Japan FY2027 draft budget Cabinet approval
catalysts.rationale: Dated to late December on the FY2026 precedent and flagged as approximate. Ministry requests total roughly JPY 143trn with a record JPY 36.6trn debt-service line struck at a 3.8% assumed rate, and the Prime Minister has said he aims to cap new issuance near JPY 40trn against JPY 29.6trn in the FY2026 initial budget. This is the event that decides whether rising Japanese yields are a policy signal or a fiscal risk premium — and a fiscal risk premium carries no currency-positive content, which is bullish for the pair.

catalysts.event: Ongoing and unscheduled: further joint Japan-US yen-buying intervention
catalysts.rationale: Dated to mid-September as a monitoring marker rather than a scheduled event. Japan has spent roughly JPY 27.1trn buying yen in 2026 against a JPY 15.32trn previous full-year record, the Finance Minister has said Japan will not hesitate to intervene jointly again, and the US Treasury Secretary repeated the commitment at the G20 on 31 August. Intervention is executed against the dollar but drags every yen cross, so EUR/JPY takes the move with no official bid defending the base leg — a genuinely one-directional risk for this pair.

assumptions: spotDate is 2026-09-03, two trading sessions newer than VALUATION_DATE of 2026-09-01; every level, target, pip figure, percentage and distance-to-average is anchored to 181.14181 at 2026-09-03, and no web-sourced quote has been substituted anywhere. The direction verdict was scored against a market at roughly 185.72 on 1 September, so a 4.58-yen gap exists between the scoring pass and this report's price anchor.

The dossiers themselves carry a third spot, EUR/JPY 185.46036, from their own 2026-08-28 store tail; where dossier figures are referenced they are quoted with that provenance and are not mixed into any calculation against the payload spot.

All moving averages, support/resistance zones and 200-week figures are computed over the full stored history (2007-12-24 to 2026-09-03, 4879 weekday bars), not over the 130 visible daily bars; the 130 bars are used only for recent price-action narrative and higher-high/lower-low structure.

Implied volatility is an estimate, not a quote: EUR/JPY has no listed option, so the payload's impliedVol block is derived from a triangle variance identity fed a realised correlation of 0.5062, documented to understate by a median 14.4% across seventeen pairs (8.7% vs EUR/GBP, 17.8% vs EUR/CHF). No one-year IV percentile could be sourced and none is asserted.

Forwards are derived, not dealer-quoted: 1M/3M/6M outrights computed from the payload's funding.premiumBp of -151.8bp annualised (observed 2026-08-31, CME calendar-spread cross), applied linearly on actual/365 basis. The premium is interest differential plus cross-currency basis and cannot be separated without an OIS curve, so the ~-27bp basis is an inference.

Rate block provenance: policy rates as of 2026-09-01; both 10-year yields are MONTHLY series as of 2026-06-01 and must not be quoted as live levels; where live levels appear (JGB 3.00% vs Bund 3.29-3.30%) the comparison is cross-dated and labelled an approximation.

Weight adjustments (Factor 10 reduced 0.04 at both horizons, released 0.02 each to Factors 1 and 6) are within the ±0.05 framework limit and both columns sum to exactly 1.00; all other factors run at framework default.

Bilateral trade figures taken verbatim from the supplied IMF DOTS block for 2024; a mirror-statistics divergence exists between EUR-reported and JPY-reported figures and the EUR-reported net of +USD 3.6bn is used, with the discrepancy disclosed.

Support/resistance zones are the payload's computed zones (clustered from weekly/monthly swing closes with touch counts) and were not supplemented from technical-analysis sites, with one disclosed exception: the 175.26-175.41 retracement cluster is web-sourced from ActionForex because the store's zones leave a genuine 4.57% void between 181.30 and 173.39.

The ten factor stances, confidences, evidence types, weights, weighted contributions, net scores, convictions, rationales, G10 rankings and consensus/cross-horizon analyses are carried verbatim from the pass-1 Direction Verdict, scored without sight of the price payload by design; nothing has been re-scored to accommodate the chart. Disagreement with the chart is stated in prose and reflected in sizing/scenario weighting, not in factor scores.

Both underlying dossiers self-flag data limitations that propagate here and were not re-verified, including a stale/unreproducible BIS REER figure, uncited September FOMC pricing, uncited IMF debt/deficit figures, and a single-source EUR/JPY risk-reversal reading from the JPY dossier's Saxo observation of 2026-09-01.

CFTC figures for the two legs use different taxonomies (euro legacy non-commercial, yen leveraged-fund) and percentile comparisons are each leg against its own history, not a like-for-like contract comparison.

Scenario probabilities (50/25/25) and price targets at both horizons are the author's structured estimates, internally consistent and summing to 100%, but are judgements rather than market-implied figures. Expected-value calculations use the forward-implied 151.8bp annualised carry rather than the 125bp policy differential.
